..
Issued at 1044 PM CDT Sat Sep 26 2026

Tonight and Sunday...

Water vapor imagery and objective analysis this evening depicts 
broad mid-level ridging over the central CONUS, sandwiched between 
an incoming western trough and nor'easter. A few peaks of sunshine 
have allowed afternoon highs to reach the mid 70s at most locations 
earlier today, though saturated soils and continued low-level 
moisture advection kept dew points in the mid 60s, creating a rather 
muggy day. 

Attention now turns to overnight fog development as a corridor or 
surface high pressure slides into northeast Nebraska, calming winds. 
As previously alluded to, grounds remain saturated with moist low-
level profiles, bringing the first of what will likely be several 
days of overnight/morning fog. Widespread fog is expected to develop 
overnight, with areas of dense fog expected, especially towards east-
central and northeast Nebraska where winds remain the calmest. 

Fog and lingering low-level stratus will be slow to break up and 
improve after daybreak Sunday. Sunshine through the day will likely 
be limited to a few pockets, with highs peaking in the low to 
mid 70s. Scattered, light rain showers and patchy drizzle is 
expected Sunday afternoon (15-20% PoPs). Accumulations will be 
limited to a few hundredths of an inch. Fog development is 
expected again into Monday morning, with patchy areas of dense 
fog possible. 

Monday... 

Another round of morning fog is expected to gradually improve after 
sunrise on Monday, before a weak shortwave disturbance brings 
another chance for scattered showers (15-30% PoPs). Mostly cloudy 
skies will keep high temperatures confined to the low to mid 70s. 
Precipitation chances increase again late Monday evening into 
Tuesday.

Tuesday and Beyond...

Into the work week, an amplifying mid- and upper-level trough will 
dig into the Desert Southwest before becoming cutoff and slowly 
tracking northeast through the Plains and into the region. Ahead of 
the system, strong moisture advection will pull into the region from 
the gulf, while the remnants of Hurricane Polo will also get swept 
up into the flow later in the work week to aid in the fairly 
impressive moisture profiles. 

The incoming system will push a cold front into the region late 
Monday into early Tuesday, bringing the first round of 80-95% PoPs. 
The front will then stall draped across north-central Kansas into 
southeast NE and southern Iowa. Additional piece of shortwave 
energy and pulses in the LLJ will support multiple chances of 
showers and storms through the work week. PWAT values will be 
impressive for late September, in the 1.70-2.00 range (maximized
across southeast NE and southwest IA). The repeated rounds of 
rain on already saturated soil will bring a flooding concern. 
Flash flooding remains possible, though exact rainfall rates and
gaps in precipitation will determine how widespread the concern
is. The larger concern will likely be area river and stream 
flooding. 

The continued cloud cover will keep high temperatures generally in 
the 60s with overnight lows in the upper 50s. PoPs of 40-75% 
continue through Thursday, with the highest values across southeast 
NE and southwest IA. Rainfall totals are expected in the 2-4" range 
through the period, support by both NBM and WPC QPF guidance.
Limited instability through the period will limit the potential
for strong to severe storms. 

Looking further ahead, the trough is expected to pull to the east 
next weekend, sweeping away the precipitation chances and cloud 
cover with it. Zonal to northwesterly flow is expected to return 
behind the system, keep cooler highs generally in the 60s. Under 
this pattern, CPC's 8-14 precipitation outlook (Valid October 4-10) 
leans below normal (40-50% probability).
